rationale: A wins because it finds real additional newsrooms without snapping the facts: "The unlikely material behind On's shoe-recycling bet: castor beans" is not the same story as the ESG, finance, or customer angles. B is disciplined and its "On turns running shoes into a subscription you never own" angle is strong, but it stops at the three obvious doors and even says the category story is "the most defensible"; that is tidy, not as useful.
gaps_in_A: "moving a core product line to this model" overstates the update. The facts say Cyclon is going nationwide, not that On is moving a core product line to subscriptions.
"does the rest of the running category have to follow?" is the weakest angle. It needs competitor evidence before it earns that big category-pressure frame.
"servicization" is trade-jargon sludge. The angle works, but that word belongs in a consultant deck, not a reporter-facing strategy note.
gaps_in_B: It leaves a viable beat on the table: B says the other angles "drop to the material" but never gives the castor-bean material its own materials-science or sustainable-manufacturing angle.
"The hook isn't the shoe" is too dismissive. A runner/subscriber behavior story is one of the cleanest human angles in the update.
"Not for sneaker-hype/streetwear press" swats away the wrong room. Running-footwear trade and athletic-industry reporters are plausible; B misses that competitive-category lens.

"Next step: `meanest-editor` ... draft a tight pitch" is the wrong handoff. The next operational move is beat selection and journalist fit-checking after chasing the missing fee and recycling-rate facts.
